books.section: Topic 4.4 America on the World Stage

stimulus.source_note: James Monroe, Seventh Annual Message to Congress, December 2, 1823; public domain.
stimulus.text: President James Monroe, in his annual message to Congress, December 2, 1823: “...the occasion has been judged proper for asserting, as a principle in which the rights and interests of the United States are involved, that the American continents, by the free and independent condition which they have assumed and maintain, are henceforth not to be considered as subjects for future colonization by any European powers...” He added: “We should consider any attempt on their part to extend their system to any portion of this hemisphere, as dangerous to our peace and safety.” He added: “With the existing colonies or dependencies of any European power we have not interfered and shall not interfere.”

source: original; stimulus quoted verbatim from James Monroe, Seventh Annual Message to Congress, December 2, 1823, public domain
stem: Which of the following best states the main point of Monroe's message?

options.text: The United States would send its army to free the colonies Europe still held in the Americas.
options.misconception: Monroe said the United States would not interfere with colonies Europe already held.

options.text: The United States would join Britain in ruling the new republics of Latin America.
options.misconception: Monroe spoke for the United States alone; he claimed no shared rule with Britain.

options.text: Europe should found no new colonies in the Americas, and new intervention would threaten the United States.
The United States would stop all trade with Europe until European armies left the Americas.
options.misconception: Monroe said nothing about cutting off trade; his warning was about colonization and intervention.

rationales.A: Monroe said the opposite about colonies Europe already held: the United States would not interfere with them.
rationales.B: Monroe spoke for the United States alone. He claimed no shared rule over Latin America with Britain.
rationales.C: Monroe draws two lines: no new European colonies in the Americas, and any European attempt to extend its system here counts as a danger to the United States.
rationales.D: Monroe said nothing about cutting off trade. His warning was about colonization and intervention, not commerce.
rationales.general:
1. Read the first line slowly. The American continents are not to be subjects for future colonization by any European power.
2. Read the second line. Extending a European system to this hemisphere would endanger American peace and safety.
3. Ask what Monroe leaves alone. Colonies Europe already holds: the United States will not interfere.
4. Put it together. The message is a warning about the future, not a promise to undo the past.
Remember: the Monroe Doctrine drew a line against new European control, not against colonies already there.
